items.title: 硅谷AI现状：谁有算力谁是爹
items.author: 量子位
items.summary:
没招了！硅谷为了争夺AI算力已经彻！底！疯！狂！


就连A社CEO Dario
items.text:
没招了！硅谷为了争夺AI算力已经彻！底！疯！狂！


就连A社CEO Dario Amodei也低声下气求到了对家Meta门前：


老铁，给点算力吧。。。

结果你猜怎么着，小扎婉拒，马斯克坐收渔利：


SpaceX充当英伟达GPU二道贩子，给Anthropic倒卖算力，赚得那叫个盆满钵满——


8月首份财报长势喜人，光季度AI业务收入就高达25.61亿美元，同比增长247%，环比更是翻了两倍之多。

好家伙！为了算力，硅谷这是拼了，大连横时代堂堂来袭。


甭管以前在网上互喷有多狠，台下还是要为了GW弯腰。


不弯不行啊，你看隔壁掉队的谷歌。


豪掷27亿美元请回来的顶级科学家Noam Shazeer，因为差算力，没两年就托马斯回旋跳去了OpenAI。


别人砸钱还要听个响，你谷歌纯纯做慈善来的。（doge）


反正硅谷现在是咂摸出味儿了：


人才留不留得住、模型能不能保持领先、AI能不能真金白银变现……这些问题，越来越取决于手里还剩多少算力。


GPU成硅谷硬通货


以前缺钱缺人，现在冒头的是算力经济。


即便强如谷歌这样的科技巨头，也无法保证明星研究员能获得足够的GPU资源。

提起Noam Shazeer，最先想到的是Transformer八子之一，他于2021年离开谷歌创立Character.AI，致力于开发生成式AI聊天机器人。


2024年，谷歌斥资27亿美元，通过交易促成Shazeer回归，并担任Gemini联合负责人。


这样的研究员，本该是巨头争相保障资源的人。


但根据外媒最新报道，他的团队同样遭遇了算力被重新分配的艰难处境，Shazeer被迫转投对家OpenAI。


无独有偶，此前哈萨比斯也曾长期对项目算力不足表达过不满，在一定程度上也影响了他卸任DeepMind CEO的决定。


目前谷歌内部，关于资源分配存在较大分歧，谢尔盖·布林有时会直接介入，将资源重新调配给自己认为重要的项目。


但归根结底还是算力资源不够，只能开源节流。


公司外部的竞争，则让行业关系变得愈加复杂。


OpenAI、Anthropic这些顶尖初创不仅要拼模型能力，还要争夺数据中心、服务器和供电能力。

以Anthropic为例，其模型的算力需求已经大到，需要与另一家模型公司讨论供货。


今年5月与SpaceX的合作协议规定，将在当月收获超300兆瓦的新容量，涉及22万块英伟达GPU，同时提高Claude Code和API的使用额度。


换句话说，这样做的目的就是让后端拿到更多算力供给前端。算力有了，模型强了，用户也留下来了。


于是模型公司的竞争开始出现两套同时运行的逻辑：


产品层面，大家还是争用户、争开发人才；基础设施层面，谁能及时提供资源，谁都可能成为潜在合作对象。

那么在夹缝中生存的小型AI创业公司呢？


它们的情况更具戏剧性。


这些公司难以自建数据中心，但过去，它们可以靠灵活租用AWS等云平台的GPU，按需付费。


然而随着头部AI实验室大量锁定算力资源，部分云服务商开始要求多年合约，预付款高达合同金额的30%，甚至要求创业公司寻找付款担保方。


以上种种，都让初创公司陷入了两难境地。


算力买太多，如果未来用户增长不及预期，持续消耗的现金就打了水漂；买太少，则可能因为没有计算资源处理需求而错失增长机会。


这样的情况反而催生出了一门新生意：全球算力淘金。


也就是寻找全球各地尚未充分利用的AI服务器资源，再将这些算力出租给需要的企业。


比如代表性的San Francisco Compute公司就曾跑到美国乡村旧鸡舍里收服务器，马斯克也和台积电讨论起了进一步的算力合作。


硅谷的顶级VC也开始亲自囤GPU，YC在7月为旗下创业公司推出专供的GPU集群，Radical Ventures还会帮助被投公司协调供应商合同。


这对于正在训练或部署模型的小型团队，稍微解决了燃眉之急。


AI算力争夺战失控


但堵不如疏，算力会出现这种短缺情况，其实个中原因相当复杂。

OpenAI、Meta乃至谷歌都在积极建设新的数据中心，承诺未来会提供海量GPU资源。


但模型快速增长的需求等不及，这中间的时间差，或者说画的大饼，就是公司还得继续四处找算力的原因之一。


用户使用AI的方式，也在无形之中加码了供给压力。


从今年开始，Agent开始代替一问一答成为用户使用的核心范式，连续长时的工作任务迫使服务器承担起更多的并行计算。


需求增加之后，连同芯片的租赁行情都发生了翻天覆地的变化。


SemiAnalysis今年4月公布的数据显示，H100一年期租赁合约价格，从2025年10月低点的每GPU每小时1.70美元，上涨至2026年3月的2.35美元，涨幅接近40%。

GPU堪比黄金的说法，并非空穴来风。


真正能即时交付、稳定运行的算力不足，新的算力还遥遥无期，共同造就了算力市场的困境。


于是算力霸权变得具体。


初创公司挑战行业巨头的叙事将日益凋零，即使有人有路线，计算资源不够也完蛋。


肉眼可见的是，算力正在成为AI时代的准入门槛，并强化拥有自建基础设施的大公司的优势。


可谓是算力我有，实力在手。


做AI产品的，要考虑的也变多了。既要担心产品没人用，也要担心用户增长速度超过自身算力扩张。


但困境亦是机遇，卖铲子的中间层乐开了花。


你说是吧，老黄？


本文来源：量子位

items.text:
美股三季报季正式拉开帷幕。整体数据看似亮眼，但繁荣表象之下暗流涌动——盈利高度集中、成本压力上升、市场对"超预期"的容忍度已大幅下降。


据美银证券的最新报告，本季市场共识预期标普500三季度每股盈利同比增长27%，美银自身预测更高，为32%（对应每股93.50美元）。早期报告公司中有85%超出每股盈利预期，高于71%的历史平均水平，宏观背景总体仍属有利。

然而，随着大型银行摩根大通、高盛、富国银行、花旗集团相继于本周登场，本轮财报季的核心矛盾将逐步浮出水面：在经历过去两个季度的大幅超预期之后，"超预期"本身已成为市场的新常态，能否推动股价上涨？


美银数据显示，2026年第二季度，标普500成分股中有77%超出每股盈利预期——这是2021年以来最高的胜率。但市场反应已明显钝化：在同时超出盈利与营收预期的公司中，其次日相对标普500的超额表现仅为0.7个百分点，约为历史均值1.4个百分点的一半；而一旦同时未达预期，股价次日平均跑输指数3.3个百分点，略高于历史均值的惩罚幅度。这一不对称性清晰传达出一个信号：市场对好消息的奖励已趋于吝啬，对坏消息的惩罚却丝毫未减。

美银警告，对于投资者而言，本次财报季的真正风险，或许不在于业绩本身，而在于三重隐形杀手：商品成本侵蚀利润、AI叙事兑现存疑、以及2027年预期过于乐观。

盈利集中度创历史极值，中位股增长近乎停滞

表面上，本季度财报季颇为可观：共识预期11个行业全部实现正增长，这在历史上仅为第二次出现。但将指数拆解后，画面截然不同。


据高盛数据，标普500前10大盈利贡献股预计将贡献本季度指数总盈利增长的68%，较一季度的47%和二季度的48%大幅跃升。


其中，美光科技（Micron）单独贡献指数增长的19%，英伟达（Nvidia）贡献15%，仅此两家合计便占三季度指数盈利增长的34%。其余贡献者依次为Meta（7%）、谷歌母公司Alphabet（6%）以及博通（Broadcom，5%），此外还有受中东冲突油价冲击受益的埃克森美孚、雪佛龙和Marathon Petroleum。


对于其余大多数公司而言，繁荣正在消退。共识预期标普500中位股三季度每股盈利增长仅为9%，低于二季度的14%，分析师预计"除信息技术和通信服务外，所有行业均呈现环比减速"。在利润率层面，分析师自本季度初以来已将中位股三季度利润率预期下调11个基点，"除信息技术外，每个行业均被下调"。


高盛的市场广度数据同样印证了这一分化：尽管标普500指数距历史高点仅2%，但中位股仍较历史高点低17%，市场广度已降至互联网泡沫以来的最低水平。

三大"隐形利润杀手"：成本、汇率与盈利质量

第一杀手：商品与能源成本侵蚀利润空间。


标普500企业在财报电话会议上提及"原材料成本"的频率已升至2022年中期以来最高水平。美银分析师指出，大宗商品通胀将在特定行业限制利润率超预期的空间。三季度美国零售汽油价格同比上涨约30%，对零售、运输、工业品等行业的成本端形成直接压力。消费者可选行业分析师Chris Nardone指出，油价若长期维持高位，利润率将面临持续风险，零售商可能被迫在转嫁价格与维护客户价值感之间做出艰难取舍。

值得注意的是，劳动力成本才是对整体指数利润率影响最大的变量——劳工支出占美国企业运营成本约40%，而能源成本占比不足5%。美银认为，目前工资通胀处于降温通道，这是对整体利润率的重要缓冲，但若能源价格持续上行并最终传导至消费端，4季度和2027年的下行风险将不可忽视。


第二杀手：AI资本支出叙事悬而未决，兑现路径仍不明朗。


超大型云计算厂商（微软、亚马逊、谷歌、Meta、甲骨文）2026年资本支出预计同比增速超过90%，远超历史任何时期，且相关2026年资本支出预测在过去一年内被上修了70%。


然而，这批公司的资本支出占运营现金流的比例已在2026年超过100%，自由现金流与净利润的背离正在扩大。美银警告，AI投资能否成功货币化，是指数盈利持续性的核心变量，而"地缘政治、利率与科技行业之间的交互影响可能被市场低估"。

大型软件分析师Tal Liani指出，进入三季度财报季，市场焦点在于软件厂商能否将客户对AI的采用转化为实质性营收增长。"需求继续超过供给，定价趋势依然有利"，但Koji Ikeda同时提示，市场将越来越多地区分真正能从AI中实现营收增长的企业，与那些仅仅依赖AI叙事的公司——"两者将出现明显分化"。


第三杀手：盈利质量存疑，一次性收益掩盖真实水准。


二季度标普500每股盈利同比增长50%，但剔除亚马逊和谷歌的私募投资重估收益后，实际增速降至32%。美银指出，这类投资重估收益"同样可以在估值反转时造成伤害"，是需要投资者穿透报表数字审视的关键变量。在指数层面，自由现金流相对净利润的比率已降至历史偏低区间，主要原因正是超大型厂商因大规模资本支出导致自由现金流承压。

2027年预期：共识乐观，美银预测更审慎

市场的真正压力测试在对未来的定价。共识预期2027年标普500每股盈利同比增长16%，显著低于2026年的33%，而美银的预测更为保守，仅为12%。


美银策略师指出，"历史数据显示，当每股盈利增速高于趋势水平但开始减速时，股票回报率历史上最为疲弱"——这恰好是当前市场所处的位置。与此同时，2027年共识预测假设"除能源行业外，所有行业均不会出现息税前利润率收缩"，在大宗商品价格高度不确定的背景下，这一假设的脆弱性显而易见。


在行业层面，信息技术（尤其是半导体）预计仍将是2027年指数盈利增长的主要驱动力，贡献约80%的增长份额，而通信服务板块在高基数效应下将面临同比负增长压力。银行股方面，美银分析师Ebrahim Poonawala指出，银行股指数BKX自8月中旬高点已下跌12%，利率上行、AI资本支出周期的持续性存疑以及AI颠覆隐忧是主要压制因素，"若这些问题的能见度能够改善，年底前存在估值修复空间"。


综合而言，本轮财报季的基本面底色依然稳健，但"超预期"的市场溢价已大幅压缩。对投资者而言，关注点应从"能否超预期"转向"超预期之后能否维持"——而成本侵蚀、AI货币化路径与2027年盈利假设，正是决定这一答案的三条关键主线。

AI硬件反弹，电路板、覆铜板、光模块等概念股大涨，天孚通信涨超7%、中际旭创早盘跌破700元后午后翻红，联讯仪器重夺A股"股王"宝座。核心逻辑是光通信公司业绩大幅预增形成"业绩兑现"催化。此外，江淮汽车盘中拉升9%，尊界V800检测报告出炉。

10月13日，A股三大指数探底回升，早盘持续下跌，创业板、科创50指数均一度跌超3%，临近午盘有所回升，午后三大股指持续拉升并翻红，创业板更是一度涨超1%，随后回落，沪指重新站上3800点，深成指、创业板小幅下跌。元件、CPO/PCB、光通信、军工装备、冰雪产业、分散染料、零售、白酒等涨幅居前；电池、风电设备、固态电池、钠电池、生物制品、电力设备等跌幅居前。

港股全天走势分化，恒指探底回升，午后拉升翻红，恒科指午后跌幅收窄至1%下方，早盘一度跌近3%，权重科网股、芯片股多数下跌，兆易创新、华虹宏力等纷纷下挫。AI大模型股同样承压。债市方面，国债期货多数反弹。商品方面，国内商品期货普遍下跌。

A股：截至收盘，沪指涨0.10%，深成指跌0.25%，创业板指跌0.18%。

盘面上，个股涨跌互现，全市场超2900只个股上涨。今日成交1.69万亿。沪深两市成交额1.68万亿，较上一个交易日放量近1400亿。板块方面，午后AI硬件侧继续活跃，军工、海运板块发力，银行、保险板块走软。动力电池、医药、房地产板块全天低迷，石化、煤炭、农业板块较为强势。

港股：截至收盘，恒指收涨0.3%，恒生科技指数跌0.79%。

盘面上，四大行齐创新高。油气、石化、交通运输、有色金属板块走强。半导体产业、人工智能主题、医药板块调整，中际旭创、立讯精密盘中创新低。

债市：国债期货全线下跌，截至收盘，30年期主力合约持平，10年期主力合约涨0.06%，5年期主力合约涨0.04%，2年期主力合约涨0.01%。

商品：国内商品期货多数下跌，截至收盘，化工品跌幅居前，纯碱跌3.42%；农副产品多数下跌，红枣跌2.58%；基本金属多数下跌，氧化铝跌2.15%；新能源材料多数下跌，碳酸锂跌1.67%；非金属建材全部下跌，玻璃跌1.50%；航运期货全部下跌，INE集运指数(欧线)跌1.48%；黑色系多数下跌，铁矿石跌1.10%；贵金属全部下跌，钯跌1.07%；油脂油料多数下跌，豆二跌0.88%；能源品涨幅居前，低硫燃料油涨5.92%。

CPO/PCB/光通信：业绩预增引爆V型反转，算力硬件年内第二波行情前奏

早盘CPO、PCB指数一度跌超4%，午后在业绩预告催化下V型反转、由跌转涨，CPO指数收涨2.21%、光通信板块收涨2.52%。

个股层面，迅捷兴、金百泽20CM涨停，协和电子、超声电子、澳弘电子、中京电子、依顿电子、骏亚科技等十余股涨停，则成电子、本川智能、满坤科技涨超10%。

龙头方面，天孚通信涨7.48%报246.70元，中际旭创早盘一度跌破700元、午后翻红收涨1.45%，新易盛涨1.06%，源杰科技涨3.64%；联讯仪器涨4.37%，市值重回2000亿元上方、重新超越贵州茅台夺回A股"股王"宝座，华盛昌涨停，太辰光、东田微等涨超5%。

催化逻辑清晰指向"业绩兑现"这条主线。10月12日晚间，联讯仪器预告2026年前三季度归母净利润19亿—21亿元，同比增长1866%—2072.95%，公司表示受益于人工智能技术快速发展及全球算力需求持续提升、数据中心建设加速推进，高速光通信领域市场需求保持较快增长，带动光模块及光芯片厂商持续扩产；源杰科技预告第三季度净利润同比增长578.85%—659.70%。

PCB链同样密集预喜，超声电子预计三季度净利润环比增长181%—206%（覆铜板产品订单充足、售价上行），广合科技预计前三季度净利润同比增长100%—107%，景旺电子第三季度净利润同比预增205%—265%，鸿富瀚前三季度净利润同比预增108%—145%，中国巨石前三季度净利润同比预增100%—110%。

对于业绩变动原因，超声电子称，主要系覆铜板行业维持高景气，行业呈现量价齐升态势，公司覆铜板产品订单充足，产品售价上行，盈利能力提升；印制板业务持续优化产品结构，产能利用率提高，综合带动净利润同比大幅增长。

这一串业绩预告共同指向一个事实：AI资本开支已越过芯片环节、向光通信与PCB等硬件产业链扩散，此前因估值消化而调整的算力硬件股迎来"业绩"与"资金"的双轮驱动回补。

国金证券指出，光博会验证了NPO/CPO产业化加速，光模块用量及价值量持续提升，定制化芯片趋势下光模块用量提升，叠加国产大模型商业化加速与国产芯片持续迭代，共同驱动国内算力产业链景气。

中信证券研报强调，铜互联逼近物理极限，Scale-up（服务器集群内部互联）"光进铜退"成为大势所趋，NPO/CPO驱动无源器件价值重估；用量方面FAU与光引擎形成1:1刚性配套、随Scale-up纯增量放大，价格方面高通道、工艺、光纤、可插拔四重溢价推动FAU价格攀升，国内无源厂商以代工/合作绑定海外头部客户，核心壁垒在于高精度制造与规模化交付。

军工股午后拉升

午后，国防军工板块涨势凌厉，航发科技率先涨停，国科军工、洪都航空、理工导航、江龙船艇、内蒙一机、中航西飞、中航成飞大幅上扬。

消息面上，据央视新闻午后报道，第十六届中国国际航空航天博览会将于2026年12月7日至13日在广东珠海举办。本届航展展览规模再创新高、国际合作广度持续拓展、展演维度加快延伸，中国空军、海军多型新型装备将同台亮相，新质战斗力建设成果成体系呈现，充分展现人民军队开放自信、捍卫和平的良好形象。

此次航展，空军多型主战装备将首次亮相，重复使用火箭将展出，无人机与反无体系化展演平台也将亮相。值得注意的是，高栏港展区是本届航展首开的展区，中国海军将依托高栏港近千米岸线打造海上装备沉浸式展示阵地，静态展出现役舰艇，并在陆地展示两栖装甲车等装备。

中船集团拟派出含新型500吨级无人舰艇在内的多型水上装备及陆上装备参展，在主场馆核心区域展出约150余项展品，并在高栏港展区同步设置动态展演区，实现“室内静态展示+室外动态展演”双场联动。

另外，军工企业规模化集中采购订单落地节奏加快，2025年末至2027年将迎来多批次、规模化装备采购订单密集落地窗口。

东方证券认为，近期，中航工业集团携全谱系多型航空装备参加2026年阿塞拜疆国际防务展、马拉喀什航展，其中阿塞拜疆航展是首次参展亮相，集中展现了我国航空装备体系化发展成果，强化在北非等市场的精准营销力度，为进一步深耕航空外贸市场注入新动能。

冰雪经济再爆发

冰雪旅游概念股集体走强。晶雪节能盘中直线拉升，走出20cm涨停。大连圣亚、冰山冷热、龙江交通、长白山等涨停。

消息面上，10月12日，第二十八届哈尔滨冰雪大世界首次官宣。据介绍，本届园区面积将扩大至125万平方米，较上一届增加5万平方米，创下历届哈尔滨冰雪大世界的规模新高；用冰用雪量突破40万立方米。园区将围绕冰雪景观、游乐体验、演艺活动、冰雪赛事、主题IP、配套服务六大板块，打造沉浸式冬日冰雪旅游盛宴。

天风证券表示，冰雪经济是从自然资源优势向产业经济价值的转化冰雪经济以冰雪运动为核心引领，通过产业链条延伸带动文化、装备、旅游相关产业协同发展，是全产业链深度融合的综合性经济形态。根据国家顶层设计，冰雪经济已正式被定位为我国国民经济新的增长点，旨在将传统的冬季“冷资源”转化为驱动内需的“热经济”，成为助力经济社会发展的新引擎。

江淮汽车盘中涨9%

江淮汽车低开高走，盘中一度涨9%，收涨超4%。

针对制动踏板争议，今日尊界汽车发布《尊界V800制动踏板检测情况说明》。说明显示，2026年10月11日，国家认可的第三方检测机构对尊界V800制动踏板进行检验，尊界V800符合行标QC/T 788-2018要求(纵向力1500N，位移量<5mm)，并做加严检验至纵向力3000N后，未出现裂纹和损坏。

此前报道显示，10月8日，懂车帝发布测试视频称，3台行驶里程极短的新车（其中1辆行驶里程不超过3km），在封闭场地进行100km/h至0紧急制动测试时，刹车踏板支架均发生断裂。

同日，尊界汽车发布关于制动踏板支架底座相关问题的情况说明。该说明称，尊界汽车的制动系统，按照高于国家标准（GB 216702025/ GB 72582026）、高于行业标准（QC/T 7882018）的要求完成全流程开发与验证。自首批车辆交付以来，在用户实际使用场景中，未发生制动踏板支架底座断裂故障。

items.title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water

items.text:
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.

There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.

"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.

People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.

Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.

But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.

This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.

Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.

But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.

"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.

"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.

A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.

People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.

While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying – engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.

Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.

It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.

But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño.

Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs.

Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest.

"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."

Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements.

Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC.

Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry.

Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere.

Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions.

Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume.

Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors – from the US, China, Australia, Singapore – because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes.

Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres with around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory".

By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates.

The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment.

Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs.

"Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages.

"We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC.

"Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

items.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
items.summary: Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr
items.text:
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.

He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."

"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.

Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.

On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.

Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.

Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".

On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.

Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".

Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".

"That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said.

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.

In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.

Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.

However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."

Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."
Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman, BBC Verify

A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together Active Memory and Active Focus to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.

Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in Muse, and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse.

Scaling Toward Personal Superintelligence

Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.

When we introduced Muse Spark, we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.

Frontier Capabilities

Model Highlights

The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.

For more details about our evaluations, see our report.

The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.

Domain Expertise

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.

Active Memory

One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory: carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

Active Focus

Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. Active Focus describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.

Frontier Coding

Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.

Kitchen GameWellness SupportInsurance Claim

Kitchen Game

Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs.

Capabilities That Generalize

Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.

To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).

Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.

Saturday Run PlanningPersonalized GiftsWedding Seating Chart

Saturday Run Planning

Play Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration.Play

Show captions for Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration.Show captions

Working directly in a browser and across apps, Muse Wonder builds a running plan (Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors) based on personal preferences and circumstances.

Muse Wonder designs and orders custom swag based on real photos taken from a personal Instagram profile.

Muse Wonder prepares a custom wedding seating chart based on a list of complex matching requirements.

Safety at the Frontier

Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.

As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework.

Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.

We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come.

items.author: whimblepop
items.summary:
What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex, Linux (WSL2)

What feature would you like to see?

Please make
items.text:
What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex, Linux (WSL2)

What feature would you like to see?

Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false) for the CLI, or at least ask once before turning it on.

Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session:

Starts a persistent background daemon (codex app-server --managed-daemon). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot.

Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex, codex-code-mode-host, bundled bwrap/zsh/rg) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/<version>/ — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager.

Starts a detached updater (codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled #40969).

Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. Hooks in --remote mode receive the daemon's cwd, not the session's #42457 and Hooks spawned by the app-server daemon cannot identify the client terminal, breaking terminal-targeting hooks #37537 (daemon cwd / terminal instead of the session's) look like the same root cause.

For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when the user explicitly runs codex app-server daemon start / bootstrap.

If it stays on by default, please at least:

Additional information

Bug found while turning it off: codex app-server daemon stop stops the app-server but leaves the pid-update-loop updater running (still alive 70 s later, had to kill it manually).

Workaround I'm using:

codex features disable daemon_auto_start
codex app-server daemon stop
pkill -f 'app-server daemon pid-update-loop' # not stopped by `daemon stop`
rm -rf ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon

With the flag off, a new TUI session no longer spawns a daemon.

Related: #40969, #41188, #46468, #48050, #42457, #37537

@Yihua-Liu-1997 thanks for reporting this, I hit it myself... stuff should not be creating mystery servers and processes all of a sudden on small version number bumps without giving people a heads-up...

agreed. the CLI is unusable until this is fixed.

I can confirm this on Windows 10 LTSC with Codex CLI 0.157.0
Setting daemon_auto_start = false in config.toml resolves the issue

Two improvements would help:

Automatically fall back to local mode when daemon startup is blocked by elevation, instead of requiring --no-daemon.

Make daemon auto-start opt-in rather than the default.

This would preserve the security restrictions without disrupting the normal CLI workflow.

@tagorr Indeed — both 1 and 2 would work~

codex: disable daemon auto-start by default

The Codex CLI is unusable due to this bug on Windows.

This is terrible. I can't input anything on the CLI at all. You should fix this problem as soon as possible and give us 100 banked reset!

There is a useful provenance boundary behind this request:

installed CLI identity != daemon execution identity

Once the CLI copies itself into a managed release directory and a background updater can replace that copy, the process that services a later turn is no longer necessarily the artifact the user explicitly installed or invoked.

I would make the daemon expose a small execution receipt for each client attachment containing at least:

client_cli_version + daemon_binary_digest + daemon_generation + updater_state + inherited_environment_generation

Then a client can distinguish:

same installed artifact, same daemon generation;

same CLI but different daemon generation;

daemon binary changed independently of the package-manager state;

daemon inherited environment from an earlier session.

A strong regression would start the daemon under environment A, attach from environment B, update the installed CLI, and verify that the client can see exactly which daemon generation/binary/environment is authoritative for the turn rather than inferring it from the foreground CLI version.

Related runtime behavioral-integrity work: https://github.com/AETHERXGLOBAL/execsurface

Update codex to 0.160.1 with a sandbox patch for nix-user-chroot

feat(codex): package Codex CLI from official release binaries

Add Oct 12 tech news (incremental scan window 18:00-19:00 UTC Oct 12 …

Basically - a trait of malware. TBF I don't even think this was done by accident

Basically - a trait of malware. TBF I don't even think this was done by accident

Honestly, that's exactly what it feels like.

The part in the docs about wanting full read/write access to the entire host filesystem is why I'm running codex-cli in a hardened Raspberry Pi and ssh'ing into it.

No daemons running that I can see, v0.160.0 from last week.

items.title: A Modern Web App in C
items.author: prophittcorey
items.summary:

items.text:
## INTRO

If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.

Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.

Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.

## TLDR

CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.

You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.

## HOW IT WAS DONE

The stack is BCHS: OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.

There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.

There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.

There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.

There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.

Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.

OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.

I lean on three additional libraries:

libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.

libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.

libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.

Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.

libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.

SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.

Both are vendored and built as part of the project.

The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.

Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory.

## WHAT I LIKED

Fundamentals over frameworks.

CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.

There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:

Request headers.

Request methods.

Query strings.

Body data.

If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.

It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.

Clear separation of concerns.

A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.

CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.

It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.

In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).

Minimal supply chain risk.

With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.

Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015.

My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019.

Simple tooling.

I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters, and no AI.

Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile.

Open a file, read it, and you know what it does.

Great tooling is within reach.

When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C.

The maturity goes further than the tools themselves: integration is built into many editors. Vim ships with native support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug).

Writing HTML and CSS in C isn't too bad.

I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined.

All too many times have I:

Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax.

Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection.

Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama.

Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate.

It was refreshing to just write C. It isn't pretty, but neither is Tailwind.

SQLite is a breath of fresh air.

I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to.

SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal.

## WHAT I WOULD CHANGE

CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library. This means you get very little out of the box.

You need to write your own utilities to handle things like:

Cookie parsing and creation.

Query parameter parsing and validation.

Form data parsing and validation.

Escaping input for display.

I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model.

I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries).

Maybe I'll publish cgi.h as a start.

## CONCLUSION

CGI is old, but it's not forgotten.

Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily.

And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade.

Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is a commercial product running on a single binary using a serving model that was officially standardized in 2004.

It has fewer moving parts than anything I've shipped before. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

blocks.x: ## INTRO

If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology.

Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript.
Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026.
## TLDR
CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026.
You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head.
## HOW IT WAS DONE
The stack is BCHS: OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite.
There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds.
There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly.
There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API.
There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder.
Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary.

OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem.
I lean on three additional libraries:
libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark.
libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks.
libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark.
Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium.
libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies.
SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build.
Both are vendored and built as part of the project.
The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second.
Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory.
## WHAT I LIKED
Fundamentals over frameworks.
CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since.
There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts:
Request headers.
Request methods.
Query strings.
Body data.
If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI.
It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever.
Clear separation of concerns.

A modern web application typically puts a web server like nginx in front and reverse-proxies to an application server written in another language like Ruby, Python, Go, or Rust. That always felt a bit strange to me: you essentially have two web servers, and one of them is also responsible for your business logic.
CGI gives you a single web server that calls your business logic directly. It's clear who does what.
It makes debugging simpler, too. Your application is an ordinary program you can run from a shell: pipe it a request, watch stderr, step through it with gdb.

In a sense, CGI resembles serverless architecture: a supervisor invokes your code per request, hands it a bag of environment variables, and collects the result. CGI is serverless, minus the vendor (and surprise bills).
Minimal supply chain risk.
With the rise of autonomous agents and weekly attacks on package repositories, it feels reassuring to have very few dependencies.

Most modern tech stacks come with a package manager and an ecosystem to go along with it. It's convenient, but the dependency graph balloons. One or two direct dependencies can pull in hundreds of indirect ones, each maintained by somebody you've never heard of, with publish credentials protected by a password reused since 2015.

My supply chain is a C compiler and three libraries. Compromising it would require compromising libcurl... a project the entire internet watches, not a package with eleven weekly downloads and an owner who left in 2019.
Simple tooling.
I'm a minimalist at heart. I use classic Vim with zero plugins. That means no LSP, no autocomplete, no code formatters, and no AI.

Complex tech stacks demand complex tooling: they demand a language server to wade through the layers of abstraction. But this stack is simple enough a plain editor is all you need. The entire application is a directory of C files and a Makefile.
Open a file, read it, and you know what it does.
Great tooling is within reach.

When you do want tooling, it's not far. Sanitizers, valgrind, gdb, ctags, cscope... these are mature (well, geriatric) tools that have been refined for decades and they're a package install away on any system that can compile C.
The maturity goes further than the tools themselves: integration is built into many editors. Vim ships with native support for ctags, cscope and has a graphical gdb frontend (see :h Termdebug).
Writing HTML and CSS in C isn't too bad.
I was hesitant to write the entire frontend in C, but it wasn't nearly as painful as I imagined.
All too many times have I:
Fought vim to highlight Go's html/template syntax.
Fought helix to detect Go templates without breaking html detection.
Fought rustrover to recognize jinja templates for a project using askama.
Using C means there's no second language for your editor to half-detect, no mixed-syntax where highlighting falls apart, no plugin dance to get the two languages to cooperate.
It was refreshing to just write C. It isn't pretty, but neither is Tailwind.
SQLite is a breath of fresh air.
I've always defaulted to Postgres for web applications. It's a great database, but it comes with some operational burden. There's a server process to babysit and frequent releases to upgrade to.
SQLite has none of that. There's no process, no configuration, no dependencies. Your application opens the database file directly. The operational burden is minimal.
## WHAT I WOULD CHANGE
CGI is an interface between a web server and your application. There's no framework or library. This means you get very little out of the box.
You need to write your own utilities to handle things like:
Cookie parsing and creation.
Query parameter parsing and validation.
Form data parsing and validation.
Escaping input for display.
I rolled my own in a single header file (cgi.h), but I'm not convinced that was the right solution. Libraries like kcgi exist, but adopting one means buying into its API and security model.
I'd like to see a set of shared utilities that developers can drop in (like the stb libraries).
Maybe I'll publish cgi.h as a start.
## CONCLUSION
CGI is old, but it's not forgotten.
Most of the reasons we abandoned it in the early 2000s don't hold up today. Process forking isn't nearly as expensive as it was; modern kernels optimize it heavily.
And if the cost of forking ever became an issue, FastCGI is a simple enough upgrade.
Writing a modern web application in C is more than feasible— marketyour.games is a commercial product running on a single binary using a serving model that was officially standardized in 2004.
It has fewer moving parts than anything I've shipped before. I'll be reaching for this stack again.

items.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.author: layer8
items.summary:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that
LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I
items.text:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that
LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree
that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion
does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields.
And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not
make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good
judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them,
interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those
requirements also apply to LLMs.

One of my colleagues used to say, "AI is a mirror." I find that insightful:
it reflects who you are, including the curiosity, judgment, and habits you
bring to it. The questions you ask and the standards you apply to its
answers matter.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability,
reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we
evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does
not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false
division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs
substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each
operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually
carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying
inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should
generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool
when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise
is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain
unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a
proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop
directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what
to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can
make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a
summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading
teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question
their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to
examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does
not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the
person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's
anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire."
Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these
systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected
outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to
consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them
"conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to
do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it
cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator
has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and
delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That
distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than
declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

items.title: Turn a WiFi 7 Router into a 320Msps Software Defined Radio Receiver
items.author: djfergus
items.summary:
Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver.
The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320
items.text:
Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver.
The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps,
its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a
live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next
to it.

The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off
corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100
spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second).

The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this
repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on
by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by
register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands
(LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. See
docs/architecture.md and docs/roadmap.md.

Sample rates

40, 80, 160 or 320 Msps of 14-bit complex IQ on every band, independent of the LO and the filter; on band 2 also 640/2 (every other sample of 640 Msps: flat to ±155 MHz, but signals 160–320 MHz away fold in)

Bands

2.4 GHz (MT7976), 5 GHz and 6 GHz (two MT7977s); switching bands is a register write inside a running stream

Tuning

No channels: the LO is any Hz a band's synthesizer locks at (unit A: 2.081–2.748, 4.647–7.509 and 4.707–7.576 GHz), on its grid of 2.98 Hz (2.4 GHz) or 11.9–14.3 Hz steps; retuned mid-stream (about 1 ms)

Front end

AGC or manual LNA/baseband gain; analog filter 20–320 MHz

Transport

the radio DMAs into a 1 GiB ring in SoC DRAM; the kernel sends every 8 KiB slice as one UDP datagram, zero-copy, on the 10 GbE port; at 320 Msps half the slices are packed to 28 bits per sample pair on the radio's own cores to fit the link (lossless, automatic)

Host

w1700k-stream receives the export and serves the IQ stream to every consumer on the host (shared memory, complex int16, gap-tagged), with an optional correction ("flatten") of the decimation's roll-off applied to the samples themselves; w1700k-spectrum: 262,144-point FFT at 100 frames/s over every sample, browser UI, live controls; sdr-recv records the stream

2.4 GHz at 320 Msps, flattened: Wi-Fi frames and shorter hopping bursts on a
floor that stays level to the band's edges. The Stream panel shows the link
carrying 9.75 Gbit/s, half of the slices packed, and every sample transformed.

Two busy 80 MHz Wi-Fi channels at 5170–5330 MHz in a flattened 320 MHz view.

Zoomed to 24 MHz around 5250 MHz: the two channels' edges and the guard gap
between them, in 1.22 kHz bins.

Path

platform/

What runs on the SoC: our U-Boot, Linux 6.18 with board patches, a read-only BusyBox root

kernel/w1700k_sdr/

The MT7996 driver (firmware download, the DMA ring, the 10 GbE export, the firmware's command mailbox) and its unit-side clients

firmware/

Our MT7996 firmware: the ROM patch, the WM (radio bring-up and band set-up, streams, RF control) and the WA (packer)

host/w1700k/

Host control: firmware load, streaming, RF control as firmware commands; w1700k serve for the web UI

host/stream/

w1700k-stream, the host's one receiver of the export: the IQ stream in shared memory for every consumer, and the roll-off correction

host/spectrum/

The spectrum/waterfall web server

host/recv/

sdr-recv, the stream recorder

init/

Installation from stock, updates, recovery, return to stock

include/hw/

Register reference: every known MT7996, A-die and AN7581 register, as C headers

docs/

Architecture, roadmap

You need a W1700K (HW 1.x) or W1700K2 (HW 2.1), a 3.3 V USB serial adapter on
its console header, an Ethernet cable to its lan3 port for installation, and
a 10 GbE NIC on the host cabled to its wan port (10GBASE-T; an X710 with a
copper SFP+ module works) for the IQ stream. Both revisions run the same images.
Most units carry a W25N04KV NAND; some W1700K2s carry a W25N04LV (ID ef 8b 23),
which is supported but has never been run on a unit: init/install stops on
one until you pass --i-dont-care-about-nand-corruption, and asks for a raw
dump of it (init/rawdump) for the maintainers.

make # everything, from public sources (~10 min plus downloads)
make check # the test suite
sudo init/host/link up IFACE # 192.168.1.10/24 on the NIC cabled to lan3
sudo init/host/tftp-forward enable IFACE
init/install # back up the NAND, install, save the radio calibration
sudo init/host/link up IFACE10G 10.77.0.10/24 9216 # the 10 GbE stream link
host/stream/build/w1700k-stream & # the stream, for every consumer on this host
host/spectrum/build/w1700k-spectrum --controller "host/bin/w1700k serve" --listen 0.0.0.0:8073

Then open http://HOST:8073/ and press ▶. The first start loads the radio
firmware and brings the radio up (about 2 s). Without the browser, the same
operations are host/bin/w1700k load|start|band|tune|gain|filter|stop|status.

Build requirements: a C/C++ compiler, make, git, Python 3.10+, the usual
Buildroot prerequisites, clang, ld.lld, llvm-objcopy and llvm-readobj (RISC-V
firmware), openssl (firmware container encryption), and
libfftw3-dev and zlib for the stream service and the spectrum server. No vendor firmware is
downloaded or needed.

Our firmware is receive-only. It runs none of MediaTek's transmit
calibrations and keeps the MAC's transmit path disabled; a gapless watch at
5250 MHz saw nothing during a load, where MediaTek's firmware transmits a
full-power burst. Still, do not cable an antenna port straight into a
sensitive instrument without an attenuator.

Our ROM patch writes no eFuse. MediaTek's ROM patches since 2025
permanently program one eFuse gate bit on their first run (also with
MediaTek's own driver); a unit that ever ran one has that bit set.

Installation replaces the stock operating system. init/install first
copies the NAND's data to the host; keep that copy. init/restore writes it
back and returns the unit to its stock firmware.

Accessing undocumented MT7996 or AN7581 addresses can hang the SoC or wedge
the radio until a power cycle. include/hw/ marks every known hazard.

MIT, except the Linux driver and kernel patches (GPL-2.0-only), U-Boot patches
(GPL-2.0+), the driver's user-space header (GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note)
and files derived from MediaTek's mt76 driver (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). See
LICENSE.

items.author: jsomers

sense it’s the prototype of much of the activity of life. The
phenomenon is the way in
items.text:
I want to tell the story of a beautiful phenomenon in biology. In some
sense it’s the prototype of much of the activity of life. The
phenomenon is the way in which an individual cell of
E. coli forages for nutrients. This process, known as
“chemotaxis”—the “chemo-” for chemical and the “taxis” from the Greek
τάξις, for tactics—is intelligence in one of
its most elemental forms. An individual E. coli has no brain,
obviously, and is even many orders of magnitude simpler than a human
cell, and yet already it possesses something like a sense of smell,
drive, even a memory. Chemotaxis recasts E. coli not as some
aimless gut-pest but rather as an exquisitely sophisticated
physical computer.

I’m also telling this story because
I never liked the way biology was taught in high school. It was too much about the names of things. A subject so vast is
spoiled by a textbook, which can only point at the endless parade of
stuff-there-is-to-know. It’s better approached with questions—like
“what’s happening when you smell?” or ”what is a fever,
actually?”—that contemplate narrow, deep slices.

Chemotaxis is a great slice: it’s a triumph of systems biology—we
understand it holistically but also in fine detail at almost every
level. It acquaints you with many of the most important motifs in
biology, including the way in which protein structure determines
function; how membranes control the information flow into cells; and
how chemical modifications store and communicate state. It involves
one of the most sophisticated and beautiful pieces of molecular
nanotechnology, the flagellar motor. And it helps give an intuition
for how a bag of unthinking chemicals could possibly give rise to a
being.

The 30,000-foot view

The basic idea is this: E. coli “smells” chemicals it’s
attracted to with a set of nose-like receptors and decides how to
swim. Depending on what it senses, it can either use its flagellar
tails to swim forward—this is known as a “run”—or it can spin in a
random direction (a “tumble”). By running when the getting is good and
tumbling when it isn’t, the E. coli takes a meandering path
toward the attractant.

A little more detail now: there are half a dozen or so rotors on the
E. coli’s body, each controlling a long whip-like tail that
flows behind it. When all the rotors are spinning in the same
direction, the tails join together into a coil that torques the cell
forward into a run. When even one rotor is spinning against the
others, the coil unbundles and E. coli spins into a tumble.

In a uniform chemical environment, the E. coli swims in a
random walk by balancing runs with periodic tumbles. By default, a run
lasts about a second, or ten times longer than a tumble. The rate of
runs versus tumbles, and their relative duration, is carefully tuned
to balance “exploitation” and “exploration”: if runs happened too
often or lasted too long, E. coli would range too widely and
zip past its food; too seldom or too short, and it’d likely never find
food in the first place.

But how is this balance achieved? The crux of it is a signaling
molecule called CheY (pronounced “KEY-why”). CheY is constantly
bouncing around in the cytoplasm of the E. coli, interacting
with both the receptor complex (the “nose”) and the rotors, carrying
information between them. In the steady state, when CheY encounters
the receptor complex, it gets chemically modified, or
“phosphorylated,” at a certain rate to become CheY-p. Unlike the
unmodified version, CheY-p has a strong affinity for the rotors, and
when enough copies bind to one, it reverses its spin, causing a
tumble.

The trick is that when the nose detects an increase in the
concentration of attractant, that steady turning of CheYs into CheY-ps
is interrupted. As a result, fewer CheY-ps bind to the rotors; fewer
reversals take place; and so the E. coli runs more and
tumbles less. In other words, the all-important relative rate of runs
versus tumbles is determined entirely by how often the
CheY→CheY-p process churns—and this, in turn, is determined by
how much attractant is detected by the nose.

You can see this process in action in the interactive illustration.
Try altering the ratio of CheY-p (white) to CheY (blue) by adding some
attractant (pink). You‘ll end up inducing a long run.
